hints: Focus on what can actually leave solution as a solid, so think about solubility rules for calcium salts first.
Remember that hydrogencarbonate ions react with hydroxide ions to make extra carbonate ions plus water.
Now combine the added calcium ions with that carbonate, and check what happens to the ammonium, chloride and nitrate ions instead.
walkthrough:
**List what is added and what is present**

We add calcium hydroxide, so we add $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ and $\text{OH}^{-}$ ions to water containing $\text{NH}_4^+$, $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$, $\text{HCO}_3^-$, $\text{Cl}^-$ and $\text{NO}_3^-$. A precipitate must be an insoluble combination of these ions.

**Convert hydrogencarbonate to carbonate**

Hydroxide removes a proton from hydrogencarbonate to give more carbonate for precipitation:
$$\text{HCO}_3^- + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{CO}_3^{2-} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Apply solubility rules to pick the precipitate**

Calcium carbonate is insoluble, while all nitrates and all chlorides (except silver and lead) are soluble:
$$\text{Ca}^{2+} + \text{CO}_3^{2-} \rightarrow \text{CaCO}_3(s)$$ 
Ammonium with hydroxide gives soluble ammonia solution, not a solid: $\text{NH}_4^+ + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{NH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$. So calcium carbonate is the solid that forms.

options.A: Incorrect. All chlorides are soluble except those of silver and lead, so $\text{CaCl}_2$ stays in solution. Students sometimes forget this rule and assume any calcium salt will precipitate.
options.B: Correct. Carbonates are insoluble except those of Group 1 and ammonium, so $\text{CaCO}_3$ is a precipitate. The added $\text{OH}^-$ also converts $\text{HCO}_3^-$ into extra $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$, giving even more $\text{CaCO}_3(s)$.
options.C: Incorrect. All nitrates are soluble with no exceptions, so $\text{Ca(NO}_3)_2$ cannot precipitate. This is a classic recall trap.
options.D: Incorrect. $\text{NH}_4^+$ does react with $\text{OH}^-$ but it forms soluble ammonia and water, $\text{NH}_4^+ + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{NH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$, not a precipitate. $\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$ is fully soluble and is best written as aqueous ammonia.
